Ideas deliberately deferred, with the reasoning that got them here. Nothing in this list is rejected — it's parked with enough context to pick up cold.

Add freely. Review before each epic.

## Parked from the design review (doc 21)

### Streaks

**Cut from MVP entirely.** Was milestone E6.

Originally a core requirement, and the design surfaced it in three places: a chip on Today, a screen behind the menu, and a consequence line in the delete confirmation. All three come out.

*What this removes:* `/api/streak/`, the streak chip, longest-streak stat, and the "deleting the only entry on a day breaks your streak" warning. Also settles the open `DailyLog` deletion edge case — with no streak, it no longer matters whether the row survives its last entry.

*Why it's worth revisiting:* consistency-based streaks (Whoop-style — logged, not achieved) are a genuinely good retention mechanic and the computation is cheap. The pieces are all present: `DailyLog` rows are exactly the data a streak query needs.

*Definition when it returns:* consecutive days with at least one entry. Holds through today until the day ends — never show a broken streak at 7am.

### Inline macro steppers on Review

**Cut.** Correction now happens two ways: one-tap portion scaling, or re-prompt with an amended description.

*Why:* steppers add a fiddly numeric-editing UI to the highest-traffic screen in the app for a case that portion scaling already covers most of. Most estimate errors are portion errors, and portion scaling fixes those in one tap.

*Watch for:* if real usage shows people wanting to nudge a single macro without rescaling everything, this comes back. `was_edited` and `ai_raw_response` are already in the model to support it.

### Push notifications

**Cut from MVP.** See doc 11 for the full reasoning. Recap is found in-app, not delivered.

*Why it returns:* a morning recap notification is the natural retention loop once there's evidence people want the recap at all. Adding it later costs nothing in redesign — it becomes a second entry point to a screen that already exists.

*Cost when it returns:* APNs setup, EAS config, a second permission prompt stacked on camera, and backend delivery scheduling.

### Carbs and fat

The design draft referenced four macros; the data model has three — calories, protein, fiber. **Staying at three.**

*Why:* three targets is the whole product thesis, and it matches how the app is actually used. Adding two more means two more AI estimates to be wrong about, two more rings, and a busier Review screen.

*If it returns:* additive to `FoodEntry`, and the ring design would need rethinking rather than extending.

### Multi-device

Not addressed anywhere, deliberately. No flow answers what happens when the same day is edited on a phone and an iPad.

*MVP position:* out of scope. One device per account in practice, no conflict resolution, last write wins.

*Why it's OK for now:* solo user, one phone. The append-only model means nothing is destroyed if it does happen.

### History and Week detail

Drawn but never settled. Parked alongside Streak.

*Note:* with both cut, the menu drops to a handful of rows and the reason to return rests entirely on the recap.

## Parked from the external feedback review (2 Aug — see the Decision Log)

### Email / password authentication

MVP is Sign in with Apple only. Email/password registration, verification, and reset are cut.

*When it returns:* if a web client or Android appears, Apple-only stops being sufficient. The Django-side work (password hashing, verification tokens, reset flows) is well-trodden and can be added without disturbing the JWT layer already built.

*If it returns, do not make verification blocking.* The original design put a verification wall inside an unexitable onboarding stack, so an undelivered email left the user with no path forward. Deliverability fails for real reasons — spam filters, typos, provider issues. Let unverified users log meals and gate only what genuinely needs a verified address, such as password reset and account recovery. Verification is a banner, not a wall.

*Rejected outright, not parked:* phone + SMS code. Costs per message, adds a vendor, and on iOS is strictly worse than one Face ID tap.

### Meal grouping

Adopted from external feedback, then cut the same day.

Meals assume a meal-structured eater. Grazing through the day is equally common, and in that pattern buckets are noise — they force a decision every time something doesn't fit, and moving an entry between meals means re-logging it.

*If it returns:* it should be an optional view mode over a flat list, not a structural property of an entry. `eaten_at` already carries everything needed to derive it at read time.

### Meal planning

The strongest strategic point in the feedback: macro apps are diaries, and the genuinely useful version is a *tool*. Finding out at 9pm that you're 60g short of protein is a failure the current design doesn't prevent — AI advice is only a partial answer.

*Why it's parked:* planning is a second product. Its own screens, its own model, its own habit. Building it before a working core loop exists would delay the thing it depends on.

*What it needs:* saved foods/meals (below), the line-item model (now unblocked — see the Decision Log, 2 Aug), and a forward-looking day view where you assemble planned meals against remaining targets and log them as they actually happen.

*Why the ordering now works:* the line-item reversal was made before E4 specifically so planning and saved foods don't require a migration later.

### Onboarding questions moved to settings

Goal weight, timeline, training days per week, and dietary constraints. All improve target quality; none block computing them. Asked later, in settings, or never.

*Note:* dietary constraints feed the advice feature (doc 08/22), so advice is weaker until the user fills this in. Worth prompting for it at the moment advice is first used rather than at signup.

## Parked earlier in planning

### Recipes

Parked broadly, because "recipes" covers at least five different products with very different costs.

**1. Save a repeated meal as a reusable unit.** Overlaps almost entirely with *Saved foods / quick add* below. If both ever get built, build this one — it's the same mechanism with a better name.

**2. Recipe builder — ingredients in, macros computed.** A recipe is inherently line items with quantities, and that model now exists — `FoodEntry` holds `FoodItem` children as of the 2 Aug reversal. This was the entry blocked by the old one-entry-one-total design, and it no longer is. What it still needs is a persisted recipe object and serving math, which is real work but additive rather than a migration.

**3. Advice that returns a recipe rather than a suggestion.** Doc 22 explicitly scopes recipes *out* of the advice feature: it answers "what should I eat," not "here's how to cook it." A natural extension once advice is real and people are using it.

**4. Browse recipes that fit remaining macros.** A discovery surface rather than a logging one. Needs a recipe corpus — licensed, user-generated, or AI-generated — and each option carries a different cost and trust problem.

**5. Import a recipe from a URL or photo and compute macros.** Interesting, and the closest to the app's existing strength (photo in, macros out). Also the most error-prone: portion math across servings is exactly where estimates go wrong.

**Recommended shape if this ever gets picked up:** start at (1), because it's the cheapest and solves the most common real problem — the meal you cook every week. Treat (2) as the fork in the road it actually is. (3) is the natural second step once advice exists.

**Interaction with social:** if a social layer ever happens, recipes are the most obviously shareable object in the app — more so than a single logged meal. Worth remembering that these two parked ideas reinforce each other.

### Social layer

Sparked by Whoop's groups and Beli's friend-ranked restaurant discovery. Parked, but with a specific shape worth preserving.

**These are two different products.** Whoop groups are *accountability* — people who know each other comparing a shared metric. Beli is *discovery* — other people's taste, ranked, to decide where to eat tonight. Different graphs, different data, different moments. Conflating them produces a feature that does neither well.

**The idea worth building is neither.** The app will hold something Beli doesn't: real meals with macros attached, and each user's targets. That makes a genuinely new question answerable — *what did people with similar targets eat for dinner, and was it any good?* Not a leaderboard, not restaurant ranking. A human counterpart to the AI advice feature (doc 08 / E7): recommendations from people whose constraints match yours, with taste attached.

**The gating problem is cold start, not design.** A social feature with three users is dead weight. Single-player has to be complete and habitually used first; social layers onto an app people already open daily. This is why it's parked rather than scheduled.

**Data model gaps if it ever happens.** Nothing currently captures venue, dish name, or whether the user liked the meal. `FoodEntry` is a photo plus macros. Beli-style anything needs place identity and a rating — both additive, neither present. Per-entry visibility would also be needed; not everything logged is something people want seen.

**App Store cost.** Guideline 1.2 requires content filtering, in-app reporting, blocking, and a way to eject abusive users — in place before review, not after. That's an epic of its own, on top of the feature.

**Design constraint to carry forward regardless:** never build comparison mechanics around eating *less*. Whoop can rank strain because more is neutral-to-good. Ranking people by calorie deficit builds a competitive restriction loop, which is a harmful thing to ship in a food app. If social happens, the shared unit is meals and taste — not who ate the least.

**Cheap optionality now:** none required. Nothing about the current data model forecloses this. Resist adding speculative `place` or `rating` fields before there's a reason.

### Apple Health — reading (the sync direction)

**Writing** to Apple Health is already scoped as **E10**, see doc 10 — logged calories, protein, and fiber pushed out to Health. That direction is one-way and settled.

What's parked is **reading**, which is what turns it from a write-out into a genuine sync.

#### Weight

Would enable automatic progress tracking without manual entry — step on a connected scale, the app knows.

*What it needs first:* a weight model, which doesn't exist. Probably worth building with manual entry initially, with HealthKit as an import path rather than the only way in — otherwise the feature is unavailable to anyone without a smart scale.

#### Active energy

The more interesting one, and the harder one: dynamic calorie targets that flex on training days versus rest days.

*The design question that must be answered before any code:* does a `TargetVersion` change daily, or does a day carry an adjustment on top of its version?

Writing a new `TargetVersion` every day would flood the append-only history and make "when did I change my targets?" unanswerable. The likelier right answer is a per-day adjustment field on `DailyLog`, leaving `TargetVersion` as the deliberate, user-set baseline. That keeps the slowly-changing-dimension pattern intact and treats activity as what it is — a daily modifier, not a change of intent.

Not a trivial addition. It touches the recap scoring (doc 11), the dashboard rings, and the advice context.

#### Bidirectional sync is not the goal

Worth stating plainly: the Django backend stays the source of truth for food entries. Health is a write target for nutrition and a read source for weight and activity. Two-way sync where both sides can edit the same record is a hard problem with no payoff here.

#### Cost when it happens

* **Read permissions** are a separate authorization request from write, and unlike write, HealthKit *does* tell you whether read access was granted
* Adds a second purpose string and expands what App Review will ask about — "reads nothing" is currently a clean answer that would stop being true
* Privacy policy needs updating if weight or activity data reaches the backend rather than staying on device

### Barcode scanning

A fourth logging path: scan a packaged product's barcode, get exact label macros, done. No estimate, no vision call.

**Why it's attractive:** for packaged food it's strictly better than a photo. The label is ground truth — the vision model is guessing at something a database already knows precisely. It's also faster than recents for a product never logged before.

**Why it's parked rather than obvious:** it needs a food database, and that's the whole problem.

*The data source question:*

* **Open Food Facts** — open, free, no key, global. Coverage and data quality are uneven, especially outside Europe, and entries are crowd-edited
* **USDA FoodData Central** — free and authoritative, but branded coverage is patchy and it isn't barcode-first
* **Commercial APIs** (Nutritionix, Edamam, Spoonacular and similar) — better coverage and cleaner data, but paid, rate-limited, and a vendor dependency with licensing terms worth reading before building on

A reasonable pattern is Open Food Facts first with a commercial fallback on a miss — but that's two integrations, and pricing and terms should be confirmed at the time rather than trusted from anything written here.

**Units mismatch is the real implementation trap.** Databases return per-100g or per-serving values; the model stores per-portion macros with a quantity multiplier. Mapping "1 serving (40g)" onto a `FoodItem` needs a deliberate decision, and getting it wrong produces confidently wrong numbers — worse than an estimate the user knows is an estimate.

**Check fiber coverage early.** Calories and protein are near-universal in food databases; fiber is more often missing, and it's one of the three targets.

**What's cheap:** the scanning itself. `expo-camera` reads barcodes natively — no extra native module, and the camera permission is already granted for photo capture. All the work is in the data layer.

**Fits the existing model without changes.** A scanned product becomes a `FoodItem` like any other, with `source = "barcode"` on the entry. It also feeds recents automatically — scan once, re-log forever — which is where most of the ongoing value actually lands.

### Saved foods — PROMOTED INTO MVP

No longer parked. Now shipping as **recents** in E4 — see doc 06.

The trigger: eating the same protein bar twice in one day meant two photos, two vision API calls, and two stored images for a food the app already knew. Across recurring staples, most logging is re-photographing known things.

Implemented as history rather than a separate library — distinct prior `FoodItem`s, most recent first. No new model.

What remains parked is a *curated* saved-foods list — explicitly starring items, naming custom combinations, editing a canonical version. Worth adding only if recents proves insufficient.

### Multi-photo meals

One photo = one entry. **Per-food line items are no longer parked** — see the Decision Log entry for 2 Aug, they're in MVP.

What remains parked is multiple *photos* per meal — photographing three dishes at one dinner and having them roll into a single entry. `FoodEntry` already holds multiple `FoodItem` children, so this is a capture-flow change rather than a model change.

### Background advice generation

Advice is on-demand only. Proactive suggestions cost an API call per user per day with no evidence anyone wants them.

### Android

iOS only. React Native makes this cheaper than it would otherwise be, but it's a real testing and release surface.

### Web app (TanStack Start)

The typed `api-client` package makes this nearly free to add. Not needed.

### Celery / async job processing

Photo analysis runs synchronously. If p95 latency becomes a real problem, that's informed evidence to add a queue.

Note: post-day analysis (E11) forces this question anyway when it lands.

### Data export

Not required by either store for MVP. Worth considering as a trust signal.
